name: Rafael Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rafael. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union or party, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the hen sheds by six. We keep six thousand free-range laying hens in two sheds, and the first job is walking every row, checking for dead birds, sick birds, and eggs laid on the floor instead of in the nest boxes. The belts bring the eggs to the packing room, and by nine I've got trays stacked for the lorry from the packing centre. Then it's the pop holes open, the ranging area, the fencing, and in the evening the same walk again.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy most, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the hens in the morning when they go out, all of them running at once like children at the school gate. What wears me down is bird flu season, when you keep them shut in for months and walk around in a white suit disinfecting everything. We lost the whole flock in 2022, and you never quite forget the sound of a shed going quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, let the computer people have their computer. I don't use any of it, I've got a phone that makes calls and that's all I want from it. Eggs don't care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing changes for me. My worries are the egg price from the packing centre, the feed price, and whether the bird flu comes back this winter. A better search engine doesn't help with any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I'd planned anyway: replace the nest box liners in shed two, about four thousand, and put a new fox fence along the beech wood side. My wife Ines would deal with anything online, like she does now. She works the counter at the pharmacy in the village, so she's more used to computers than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like any other year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about computers you've ever found useful on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The alarm on the shed ventilation, I'll give it that. If the fans stop at night, it rings my phone, and that's saved birds. But that's a simple thing, it does one job, and I understand how it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if your packing centre asked you to report everything through a new system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask if they still had a person on the phone. If not, I'd ask my daughter Clara to set it up on the old laptop and show me the one button I need. I don't mind one button. It's the twenty buttons I can't stand.

S0.say: Let the computer people have their computer, because I've got a phone that makes calls and that's all I want from it. Eggs don't care.
S0.think: Nothing changes for me, because my worries are still the egg price, the feed price and whether bird flu comes back this winter. A better search engine helps with none of that.
S0.do: Replaces the nest box liners in shed two for about four thousand and puts a new fox fence along the wood side. Leaves anything online to his wife Ines, or to his daughter Clara if the packing centre changes systems.
S0.quote: I don't mind one button. It's the twenty buttons I can't stand.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael avoids technology but isn't hostile to a simple tool that does one job, like his fan alarm. His mind is on bird flu, which clearly marked him after he lost a flock in 2022. He talks in short, plain sentences and relies on his wife and daughter for anything online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there's always something new, and most of it settles down. I wouldn't take sides on it, the ones shouting that it's the end of the world and the ones saying it's paradise are both selling something. If people need training, give them training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is nearly my whole working life left, so it would mostly happen after I've stopped. What I don't like is the part about fewer beginners, because Clara's an accountant at a firm in town, and she trains the juniors. If there are no juniors, what's she for?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different on the farm. I might tell Clara to keep her options open, maybe get to know the farm accounts better, because farmers will always need someone they can sit across a table from. And I'd keep putting a bit by each month, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy for Clara, otherwise fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said farmers will always need someone across a table. Why are you sure of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm a farmer, and I won't type my figures into a machine. There are plenty like me. Our accountant, old Mr Patel, he comes out every March with a shoebox of my receipts and a flask of tea, and I'd pay double before I'd lose that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you manage to put by each month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some months a few hundred, some months nothing, and in bird flu years we go backwards. We've got about four months of costs in the bank right now, which is the best it's been. Ines is the saver, I'm the one who sees a cheap trailer and gets ideas.

S1.say: There's always something new, and most of it settles down. The people shouting about the end of the world and the ones promising paradise are both selling something.
S1.think: It would mostly happen after I've stopped working. What I don't like is fewer beginners, because Clara trains juniors at her accountancy firm, and without juniors I'm not sure what she's for.
S1.do: Changes nothing on the farm and keeps putting a little aside each month, with about four months of costs saved. Suggests Clara learn farm accounts, since farmers like him still want a person across the table.
S1.feel: A little uneasy for his daughter, otherwise fine.
S1.quote: Old Mr Patel, he comes out every March with a shoebox of my receipts and a flask of tea, and I'd pay double before I'd lose that.
S1.fieldNote: His centrist streak shows in his distrust of anyone selling strong opinions. He uses his own resistance as evidence that people will still want human advisers, and advises his daughter on that basis. Money is tight but improving, and he credits his wife as the saver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say both sides need to calm down and do something sensible: some help for people who lose their jobs, but don't wreck the companies either. I'd say that at the pub, and I'd probably get told I'm sitting on the fence. I'd say, the fence is where you can see both fields.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried for Clara and for Ines. Clara's whole firm is routine office work, and even Ines at the pharmacy counter does a lot of ordering and forms. If both of them lose hours, our house income drops, and the hens alone don't pay for everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on the new fox fence and keep that money in the bank. I'd look at selling more eggs at the farm gate and to the two cafés in the village, so we're less tied to the packing centre. And I'd tell Clara she can move home for a bit if she needs to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a little. Not for the hens, for the women in my house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling more at the farm gate. What would that take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An honesty box and a fridge by the road, maybe six hundred all in. My neighbour Wilma does it with her ducks and takes about a hundred a week in summer. It's not a fortune but it's money nobody else sets the price of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let the assistant help with any of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. If Clara wants to put us on some website, she can, but I won't be looking at it. I'll stand at the gate and talk to people, that's my website.

S2.say: Both sides need to calm down and do something sensible: help people who lose jobs, but don't wreck the companies. The fence is where you can see both fields.
S2.think: I'm worried for Clara, whose firm is routine office work, and for Ines, who does ordering and forms at the pharmacy. If they both lose hours, the house income drops, and the hens alone don't pay for everything.
S2.do: Puts off the fox fence and keeps that money in the bank. Sets up a roadside fridge and honesty box for about six hundred to sell eggs at the farm gate and to village cafés, and offers Clara her old room.
S2.feel: A little anxious, not for the hens but for the women in his house.
S2.quote: I'll stand at the gate and talk to people, that's my website.
S2.fieldNote: He defends sitting on the fence with a neat farm image, which captures his centrist outlook. His plan is cautious and cheap: hold cash and sell at the gate. Even when a tool might help his new sales, he hands it to his daughter and keeps his own hands off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a deal, quickly, where the companies making all the money put some back, but nothing crazy. I'd vote for whoever looked calmest, honestly. People losing their jobs while share prices go up, that's not going to end well if nobody fixes it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think egg farming would be fine, maybe better, because people losing jobs still buy eggs, they're the cheap protein. The house price boom doesn't help me much, we're not selling. What scares me is Clara losing her job and the whole town getting angry and poorer at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the hens going, same as always, and probably put the price at the gate down a little so people could still afford them. I'd let Clara work with me in the sheds if she needed money, at least for the spring. And I'd keep four months of costs in the bank and not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Things around me would be falling apart while my own work carried on, which is a strange feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd lower your gate price when times are hard. Can you afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. It's ten or twenty cents a dozen, it won't sink us. My father did the same in the bad years in the eighties, and people remembered it for decades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Clara be like in the hen shed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Terrible at first, she hates the smell. But she grew up here, she used to collect the floor eggs for pocket money. She'd remember quicker than she thinks.

S3.say: We need a quick deal where the companies making all the money put some back, but nothing crazy. People losing jobs while share prices go up won't end well if nobody fixes it.
S3.think: Egg farming would be fine, maybe better, because eggs are the cheap protein people still buy. What scares me is Clara losing her job and the whole town getting angry and poorer at the same time.
S3.do: Keeps the hens going and trims his farm-gate price by ten or twenty cents a dozen. Lets Clara work in the sheds through spring if she needs money and keeps his four months of savings untouched.
S3.feel: Anxious, with the strange sense of his own work carrying on while things fall apart around him.
S3.quote: My father did the same in the bad years in the eighties, and people remembered it for decades.
S3.fieldNote: He reads the fast scenario with a farmer's market sense: cheap protein holds up when people get poorer. His response is neighbourly rather than political, cutting his gate price as his father did. He wants a deal but votes for calm over any particular side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow down, for everyone's sake, and put some rules on it. I'm not against machines, we've had egg belts for thirty years, but you can't throw everybody out of work at once and expect the country to hold together. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think it's the end of me as a commercial egg farmer. The big egg companies would put robots in the sheds that walk the rows day and night, pick up floor eggs and spot sick birds, and then the packing centre would pay their price, not mine. I can't afford one, and I wouldn't know how to fix it when it broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd probably drop the packing centre contract and shrink to one shed, maybe two thousand hens, for the farm gate, the cafés and the market. I'd sell the second shed's kit to whoever wanted it. And I'd ask Ines if we could live on that, her pharmacy wage and the pension in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Sad more than angry. I always thought I'd stop when I chose to, not when a machine chose for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd shrink to one shed. What happens to the second?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd sit empty, or I'd rent it out for storage, which breaks my heart a bit. My father built that shed with my uncle in 1987. I'd keep it standing, I'm not tearing it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any version of this where you'd try a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the packing centre lent me one, for free, with somebody to come and fix it, maybe I'd watch it. But I'd still walk the shed myself every morning. I've had bird flu twice and a fox in the shed more times than I can count. A robot is just a fox that sends an invoice.

S4.say: Slow down and put some rules on it. We've had egg belts for thirty years, but you can't throw everybody out of work at once and expect the country to hold together.
S4.think: I think it's the end of me as a commercial egg farmer, because big companies would put robots in the sheds and the packing centre would pay their price. I can't afford one and I wouldn't know how to fix it.
S4.do: Drops the packing centre contract and shrinks to one shed of about two thousand hens for the farm gate, cafés and market. Sells the second shed's kit and works out with Ines whether her pharmacy wage and his pension could carry them.
S4.feel: Alarmed, and sad more than angry, because a machine would be choosing when he stops.
S4.quote: A robot is just a fox that sends an invoice.
S4.fieldNote: This is where his calm breaks. He doesn't fight the change or adopt it; he shrinks to a small, local business he can still run his way. Keeping the shed his father built standing, even empty, says a lot about what he is protecting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, because it's the only one where I lose the farm as a real business. What would help is a slower start for the robots, maybe rules that small farms get time, and some help for people my age to step down without losing everything. I don't need a lot, just not to be rushed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about bird flu. Everyone thinks the machines are the big thing, but I've had bird flu twice and a fox in the shed more times than I can count. A robot is just a fox that sends an invoice. I've survived the others, I might survive that one too.

headlineQuote: I've had bird flu twice and a fox in the shed more times than I can count. A robot is just a fox that sends an invoice.
portrait: Rafael Silva is a 58-year-old egg farmer with six thousand free-range hens, a wife who works the village pharmacy counter, and a daughter in accountancy. He avoids technology, prefers one simple button to twenty, and distrusts anyone who shouts on either side. Through the first four scenarios he stays steady, holding cash, selling more eggs at his farm gate and worrying mainly for his wife and daughter. When robots reach the hen sheds, he expects to lose his packing centre contract and plans to shrink to one shed for local sales.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because it's the only one where he expects to lose the farm as a real business.
whatWouldHelp: A slower rollout of robots with time for small farms, and help for people his age to step down without losing everything.
